The dimensions of this texture do not need to match the dynamic range of the input data channels, allowing for memory-efficient discretization [S1, book].

The evidence explicitly states that 'the ability to scale and interpolate color channel values is a convenient feature of the hardware. It allows the number of elements along a dimension of the texture containing the new color values to differ from the dynamic range of the component that generated the texture coordinate.' It further explains that without this flexibility, the texture size would be 'prohibitively large,' implying that this feature enables memory efficiency. This directly supports the claim that dimensions do not need to match the dynamic range, allowing for memory-efficient discretization.

Dependent Texture Reads (DTR) is a hardware extension that uses the color components of a fragment to generate texture coordinates, replacing the original color with values looked up from a texture [S1, book][S2].

The claim states that Dependent Texture Reads (DTR) is a hardware extension that uses color components of a fragment to generate texture coordinates, replacing the original color with values looked up from a texture. Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly define DTR in this exact manner. Specifically, they state that DTR operations 'use color fragments to generate texture coordinates, and replace those color fragments with the corresponding entries from a texture.' The sources further elaborate on the mechanism (scaling RGB values to 0-1, using them as 3D texture coordinates, and replacing original values), which aligns perfectly with the claim.

Unlike standard texture sampling where coordinates are explicit attributes, DTR derives coordinates dynamically from the fragment's RGB values, enabling arbitrary function evaluation with up to three variables [S1, book][S2].

The claim states that DTR (Dependent Texture Reads) derives coordinates dynamically from fragment RGB values, unlike standard sampling where coordinates are explicit attributes, and that this enables arbitrary function evaluation with up to three variables. Source [S1] explicitly states that dependent texture reads 'use color fragments to generate texture coordinates' and that 'This operation essentially amounts to an arbitrary function evaluation with up to three variables via a lookup table.' It further details that 'each channel value would be scaled between zero and one, and these new values would then be used as texture coordinates of a 3D texture.' Source [S2] corroborates these exact points. The claim accurately reflects the information provided in both sources.
